name: Malay, 'het Djohorsch of Riouwsch' = Johor-Riau Malay
catalog_citation: van Wijk, D. Gerth. 1890. Spraakleer der Maleische taal. Batavia: G. Kolff & Co. Sec. 95-96 'Klemtoon', printed pp. 46-48. (Glottolog's long grammar for mala1479; Inleiding sec. 1 p. III: treats only 'het Djohorsch of Riouwsch' Malay.)
catalog_locator: Sec. 95 'Klemtoon', printed p. 46 = PDF p. 70 of archive.org item spraakleer-der-maleische-taal (our source folder/…
catalog_quote: § 95. De klemtoon is in het Maleisch in het algemeen zeer zwak; alle lettergrepen, die niet geheel toonloos zijn, worden met nagenoeg denzelfden nadruk uitgesproken ... alleen op de voorlaatste of de laatste wordt wat meer klemtoon gelegd, niet zoozeer door er sterker op te drukken of de stem te verheffen, maar alleen door ze wat gerekter en langzamer uit te spreken. In het algemeen valt de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep van het stamwoord (1); alleen wanneer deze open is en een pĕpĕt heeft, komt het accent op de laatste lettergreep; dus b. v. kàta, boèroeng, tèmpat, dèndam, binàsa, bĕlàlai (2); daarentegen bĕlòm, tjĕrài, bĕnàr, pĕtjàh, djĕdjàk, bĕsàr, kĕnà, kĕnàl. Wordt echter die open toonlooze lettergreep gevolgd door ng, dan valt het accent toch meer op de penultima dan op de ultima; b. v. tèngah, dèngar; dikwijls is het bij de kleurloosheid der uitspraak moeielijk te besliss…

new_statements.quote: § 95. De klemtoon is in het Maleisch in het algemeen zeer zwak; alle lettergrepen, die niet geheel toonloos zijn, worden met nagenoeg denzelfden nadruk uitgesproken ... alleen op de voorlaatste of de laatste wordt wat meer klemtoon gelegd, niet zoozeer door er sterker op te drukken of de stem te verheffen, maar alleen door ze wat gerekter en langzamer uit te spreken. In het algemeen valt de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep van het stamwoord; alleen wanneer deze open is en een pĕpĕt heeft, komt het accent op de laatste lettergreep; dus b. v. kàta, boèroeng, tèmpat, dèndam, binàsa, bĕlàlai; daarentegen bĕlòm, tjĕrài, bĕnàr, pĕtjàh, djĕdjàk, bĕsàr, kĕnà, kĕnàl.
new_statements.translation: Sec. 95. Stress in Malay is in general very weak; all syllables that are not wholly toneless [schwa-syllables] are pronounced with almost the same emphasis ... only the penultimate or the last receives somewhat more stress, not so much by pressing harder on it or raising the voice, but only by pronouncing it somewhat more drawn-out and slowly. In general the stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; only when this syllable is open and has a pepet [schwa] does the accent come on the last syllable; thus e.g. kàta, boèroeng, tèmpat, dèndam, binàsa, bĕlàlai; on the other hand bĕlòm, tjĕrài, bĕnàr, pĕtjàh, djĕdjàk, bĕsàr, kĕnà, kĕnàl.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak durational prominence on the penultimate syllable of the root; if the penult is an open syllable whose vowel is schwa (pepet), prominence falls on the final syllable instead (schwa-light penult -> final). If the open schwa penult is followed by ng (tengah, dengar) the accent stays rather on the penult, though often hard to decide. Under suffixation the root normally keeps its stress (bànding > bàndingan, koèmpoel > koèmpoelan), i.e. the domain is the root, not the suffixed word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec.96 (p.47, quoting von de Wall): in educated/spelling-influenced speech a weak second 'grammatical' stress may appear on the new penult (long vowel) of suffixed forms beside the strong natural root stress (bàntoe, bàntoei, pĕrbàntoean); rarely the root stress is lost entirely (katànja < kàta, tambàngan ~ tàmbangan). Crawfurd 1852:cix adds that polysyllables have two accents, on the first and on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: European loans with original final accent keep it (majoòr, tamboèr); apparent antepenultimate cases manoèsia, moèlia, karoènia are really penultimate (karoènja, moèlja, manoèsja); emphasis can lengthen a schwa penult (soedah pĕtjah); shifting stress fully onto the suffix-created penult (koedànja, padànja) is called a European-Javanese habit 'never heard from the Malay'. Winstedt [1945]:4 gives the same rule for colloquial peninsular Malay ('no strong accent on any syllable'; penult, but final when penult is schwa in an open and rarely a closed syllable: sĕrì, ĕnàm, ĕntàh, ĕmpàt; root keeps its stress under suffixation). Modern instrumental work on Malaysian Malay (Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008; Wan 2012) argues the apparent penult prominence is a phrase-final pitch peak plus final lengthening and that Malay has no word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Author's domain is the root word ('stamwoord') in citation; he stresses that prominence is durational and very weak. The rule is the classic schwa-conditioned penult/final pattern (StressTyp2/Hayes treat open schwa penults as light), hence 'weight-sensitive' rather than plain fixed-penult; a no-word-stress reading is defended by modern phoneticians for present-day Malaysian Malay, so the catalog entry should carry that caution.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 'Central Malay' mala1479 [zlm] is the Greater Riau-Johoric colloquial-Malay node (dialects: Johor, Kuala Lumpur, Melaka, Selangor, Sarawak, Riau, Siak, Riau Sea Tribe, Deli, Sambas, Sedentary Belitung, Melayu Ulu Kapuas, Jambi Pesisir). It is NOT Besemah/'Central Malay' [pse] (= cent2053 South Barisan Malay, already in the catalog via McDonnell 2016); the earlier world-scan note naming McDonnell 2016 confused the two. The quoted source, van Wijk 1890, states (Inleiding p.III) that it treats only 'Djohorsch of Riouwsch' (Johor-Riau) Malay, i.e. exactly this node, and is Glottolog's MED long grammar for mala1479. Note overlap risk with the catalog's existing stan1306 'Malay' entry (Winstedt 1913 Malay Grammar, same schwa-conditioned penult rule) and with Zuraidah et al. 2008 / Clynes & Deterding 2011 (no-word-stress analyses of Standard/Malaysian Malay) held under stan1306.

sources.note: Stress very weak; falls on the penult of the root word, but on the final syllable when the penult is an open syllable with pepet (schwa); if that schwa penult is followed by ng the accent stays rather on the penult (tengah, dengar); sec.96: stress normally stays on the root syllable under suffixation (bandingan, koempoelan), with a weak secondary 'grammatical' stress on the new long vowel in educated speech; apparent antepenult cases (manoesia) are really penult (manoesja).

sources.citation: Favre, P. 1876. Grammaire de la langue malaise. Vienne: Imprimerie imperiale et royale. Accent rules printed pp.34-35 (archive.org grammairedelalan00favr scanned text).
sources.note: Accent weak, realised as slower/longer syllable; general tendency penultimate: Rule 1 penult open-long or closed -> penult (padang, kilat, bumi, pintu); Rule 2 penult open and short [schwa] -> final (beri, seru, belum, benar); Rule 3 before ng either (dengar, tengah), he prefers penult; suffixed words: either new penult or original root syllable (mendapatkan ~ mendapatkan).

sources.citation: StressTyp2 (2015 SQL dump) entry 'Malay': penult, final if penult schwa; sources Winstedt 1927 Malay Grammar and Lewis 1947 Teach Yourself Malay (already used by our catalog for stan1306).
sources.note: Second-hand: 'Main stress falls on the penult unless this is a schwa, in which case stress falls on the ultima. In Malay only open syllables with schwa are light (Hayes 1995:263)'; remark that Lewis 1947's variety has antepenult stress in heavy-light-heavy words.

sources.citation: Wan Aslynn Salwani Wan Ahmad. 2012. Instrumental phonetic study of the rhythm of Malay. PhD thesis, Newcastle University. Literature review pp.64, 68 (held from the stan1306 audit).
sources.note: Reports second-hand that Farid (1980) [Johor Malay], Baskaran (1982), Suhaila (1994) and Teoh (1994) 'claim that, based on auditory observation, there is no systematic variation of syllable prominence in Malay connected speech'; her own experiments: durational penult/final effects in isolated words vanish in connected speech.

sources.citation: Zuraidah Mohd Don, Gerry Knowles & Janet Yong. 2008. How words can be misleading: a study of syllable timing and 'stress' in Malay. The Linguistics Journal 3(2). (Two native speakers of Malaysian Malay, Univ. Malaya; held from the stan1306 audit.)
sources.note: Citation forms show an F0 peak on the penult and final lengthening, which looks like penult stress, but in connected speech this is an onset rise + final cadence of the phrase; they conclude Malay 'does not have word stress at all' and disagree with earlier penult-stress claims; schwa penult (betul) delays the peak to the final syllable.

sources.citation: Winstedt, Richard O. [1945]. Colloquial Malay: a grammar with conversations and an appendix on the Malayo-Arabic spelling. New edition revised. London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner. (Glottolog lists this title under mala1479.) 'Accent', printed p.4 (PDF p.14 of Digital Library of India scan), page image read.
sources.note: 'There is no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word. Ordinarily the stress, such as it is, falls on the penultimate... the only important exception being that when the penultimate is e-breve [schwa] in an open syllable and rarely in a closed, then the stress falls on the last syllable, e.g. seri, enam, entah, empat.' Suffixed words: root keeps its stress and the new penult is prolonged (except -kan after consonant-final stem).

sources.citation: Crawfurd, John. 1852. A Grammar and Dictionary of the Malay Language, vol. 1. London: Smith, Elder. Preliminary Dissertation p.cix (archive.org grammardictionar00craw scanned text).
sources.note: 'Accent, in the Malay, the Javanese, and other languages of the west is a very simple and easy matter. In bisyllabic and trisyllabic words, it is, with very few exceptions, on the penultimate, and in polysyllabic words, without exception, there are two accents, one on the first and one on the penultimate syllable.'

sources.citation: Marsden, William. 1812. A Grammar of the Malayan Language. London. 'Of Prosody: Of Quantity', printed p.118 (archive.org grammarofmalayan00mars scanned text).
sources.note: Long penult (of di-/trisyllable) always accented (bunoh, takut, kapala); when both syllables short the accent generally on the first, 'in all doubtful cases the accent inclines to the former'; but besar, kechil, belum (schwa penult) have 'a decided stress upon the last'; accent 'much less strong than in the languages of Europe'.
